items.title: 302 Sales to Government Agencies and Exempt Organizations (PDF) — Maine Revenue Services Rules and Rulemaking
items.content_text:
18 DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE AND FINANCIAL SERVICES 
 
125 MAINE REVENUE SERVICES 
 
Chapter 302: SALES TO GOVERNMENTAL AGENCIES AND EXEMPT 
ORGANIZATIONS
 
 
 
 
SUMMARY:  Establishes administrative rules regarding tax-exempt sales and explains 
the circumstances under which a retailer or service provider will be relieved of its burden 
of proving that sales to an entity described in 36 M.R.S. §§ 1760 or 2557, including an 
agency or instrumentality of the federal government or of the State of Maine, are exempt 
from Maine sales, or use, or service provider tax. 
 
  
SECTION 1.  Exempt sales generally; burden of proof 
 1. Generally Sales and Use Tax.  Sales to certain organizations and governmental 
agencies are exempt from sales and use tax pursuant to 36 M.R.S. § 1760.  Pursuant to 36 
M.R.S. § 1760-C, an exemption provided by 36 M.R.S. § 1760 to a person based upon its 
charitable, nonprofit , or other public purposes applies only if the property or service 
purchased is intended to be used by the person primarily in the activity identified by the 
particular exemption.  The burden of proving a sale is to an organization that is exempt 
under 36 M.R.S. § 1760 is on the person making the sale.  The retailer is relieved of this 
burden of proof if it satisfies the provisions of this rule.  
 2. Certain purchases subject to tax.  Pursuant to 36 M.R.S. § 1760- C, an 
exemption provided by 36 M.R.S. § 1760 to a person based upon its charitable, nonprofit, 
or other public purposes applies only if the property or taxable service purchased is 
intended to be used by the person primarily in the activity identified by the particular 
exemption.  If property or taxable services that were purchased exempt are used primarily 
in an activity or  activities not identified by the particular exemption, use tax liability 
accrues.   
An exemption based on charitable, nonprofit, or other public purposes  does not 
apply to any purchase for use by an exempt organization in it

items.title: Digital Archives — Maine Secretary of State — Bureau of Corporations, Elections & Commissions News
items.content_text:
Welcome to the online digital collection of the Maine State Archives, a bureau within the Department of the Secretary of State. We maintain approximately 8 miles of official state records (both paper and digital) that are deemed permanently valuable. These records include bills introduced in the Legislature, reports from the Governor's Executive Council, election returns, deeds and maps from the Maine Land Office, vital statistics prior to 1892, federal census records up to 1880, county court records dating back to 1636, and military records through World War I, among others.
As of March 1, 2026, our online collection includes over one million individual records. The Maine State Archives will continue to expand this database as we digitize more of our collection. All documents are public records and are free to download. To begin your search, check the following sources:
Digital Archives Portal
: Open Access - online digital collection of the Maine State Archives.
ArchivesSpace Public Interface
: Use this database to search through the archival findings aids, collection structures, and descriptions of physical and digital records managed by the bureau.
Maine Memory Network
: A digital history platform featuring specific exhibits, historical photographs, and selected primary documents contributed by the Maine State Archives.
Family Search
: FamilySearch is the world’s largest free genealogy resource.

items.title: Maine Logger’s Day - October 12 — Governor of Maine — Official Documents (Executive Orders)
items.content_text:
WHEREAS
, the logging industry has served as an economic driver and cultural tradition in Maine for centuries; and
WHEREAS
, the logging industry creates rural jobs and provides revenue for local communities, contributing $534 million to the state’s economy annually; and
WHEREAS
, loggers provide renewable material for products used by people in Maine every day; and
WHEREAS
, loggers are the root of Maine’s $8.3 billion forest economy; and
WHEREAS
, loggers are the means by which healthy and responsible forest management plans are accomplished; and
WHEREAS
, logging helps keep Maine’s forests healthy, which support vital animal habitats, protect watersheds, sequester carbon, provide recreational opportunities, and limit wildfires; and
WHEREAS
, logging provides for healthy forests through regeneration to ensure the sustainability of the industry for future generations of Maine people;
NOW THEREFORE
, be it resolved that I, Janet T. Mills, Governor of the State of Maine, do hereby proclaim October 12, 2026 as
Maine Logger’s Day
throughout the State of Maine, and I urge all citizens to recognize this observance.
In testimony whereof, I have caused
the Great Seal of the State to be
hereunto affixed GIVEN under my
hand at Augusta this tenth day
of September Two Thousand Twenty-Six

items.title: Maine Needham Day - September 26 — Governor of Maine — Official Documents (Executive Orders)
items.content_text:
WHEREAS
, the Maine Needham was first introduced in 1872 by John Seavey, owner of the confectionary Seavey’s Sweets, which is rumored to have been located in either Auburn or Portland at the time; and
WHEREAS
, named after a popular preacher of that era, George C. Needham, the Needham candy consists of a mashed potato center surrounded by coconut and chocolate; and
WHEREAS
, it is thought that Needhams gained popularity with home cooks during the Great Depression, when Maine people would use their extra potato harvest to make the treat; and
WHEREAS
, Needhams have become synonymous with Maine, and they help celebrate locally harvested Maine potatoes; and
WHEREAS
, today, sweet shops and home cooks around our state keep the beloved tradition of the Needham alive by continuing to produce and perfect this iconic Maine treat for us to enjoy and share with the world; and
WHEREAS
, on September 26, 2026 the fourth annual Maine Needham Festival will be held at the Maine Tasting Center in Wiscasset to celebrate the Needham and it’s great history in Maine; and
WHEREAS
, in accordance with 1 MRSA § 150-S, the State of Maine observes the last Saturday in September each year as Maine Needham Day;
NOW THEREFORE
, be it resolved that I, Janet T. Mills, Governor of the State of Maine, do hereby proclaim September 26, 2026 as
Maine Needham Day
and I urge all citizens to recognize the Needham’s history and celebrate this delectable Maine treat.
In testimony whereof, I have caused
the Great Seal of the State to be
hereunto affixed GIVEN under my
hand at Augusta this tenth day
of September Two Thousand Twenty-Six

, First Parish Church was established in 1674, the first colonial religious congregation serving the spiritual needs of the area that over 150 years later would be incorporated as the City of Portland; and
WHEREAS

WHEREAS
, the predecessor building “Old Jerusalem” was the site of Maine’s Constitutional Convention in October 1819 that led to the document strongly rooted in political independence, religious freedom and popular control of government; and
WHEREAS
, because of its stone construction, the First Parish Meeting House was one of the few buildings that survived Portland’s Great Fire of 1866, though the wooden buildings surrounding the Meeting House were consumed by the fire; and
WHEREAS
, First Parish has a long history of activism and support for equal rights throughout Maine and the Nation, including its involvement in the abolitionist movement, its leadership in anti- Ku Klux Klan activity and the Portland Freedom March, and its longstanding efforts to support and welcome the LGBTQ community; and
WHEREAS
, First Parish remains active in social justice work in Portland, including support for community food security; outreach and support for individuals who are unhoused, and support for new immigrants to Maine; and

, in 1973, the First Parish Church became one of the first buildings in Portland to be listed on the National Register of Historic Places;

200th Anniversary of the First Parish Church

Sep 16, 2026

The Maine Department of Health and Human Services’ Center for Disease Control and Prevention (Maine CDC) is reporting a case of measles in Maine; the first case in the state since five cases were confirmed in February of this year. The Maine CDC confirmed the latest case on September 15, 2026. According to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (U.S. CDC), as of September 11, there were 3,294 confirmed measles cases reported nationwide in 2026.

The individual is an unvaccinated adult from Somerset County. The Maine CDC is working with the facility where potential exposure occurred and is working with them to inform potentially exposed individuals.

Individuals who were at the following location* during the timeframe listed below were potentially exposed to measles and should take precautions and should watch for symptoms for 21 days after September 12:

Location

Date

Time

MaineGeneral Express Care, Waterville 211 Main Street, Waterville, ME

September 12, 2026

8am-11am

*Subject to change as the investigation continues

Measles is a highly contagious viral disease. If one person has measles, 90% of the people close to that person who are not immune will become infected. Symptoms of measles include:

  • Fever
  • Cough
  • Runny nose
  • Red, watery eyes
  • Rash that spreads from the head down.

Individuals who develop symptoms should contact their health care provider for instructions before going to the provider’s office or hospital. This will help prevent the spread of further infection. If symptoms are consistent with measles, a health care professional may test to determine a measles infection.

Measles can cause severe sickness including pneumonia, encephalitis (brain swelling), and death. An infected person spreads measles through coughs or sneezes. Once infected, a person is contagious from four days before their rash starts through four days afterwards. The virus remains alive for up to two hours on surfaces and in the air. The period from exposure to onset of symptoms is typically 10 to 14 days, but can be longer.

The measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine is the best prevention for measles. Individuals who:   

  • have been potentially exposed should review their vaccine history and watch for symptoms.
  • are not immunized or do not know their measles immunization status should get vaccinated.
  • develop symptoms should contact their health provider for instructions before going to the provider’s office or hospital. This will help prevent the spread of further infection.

Recommendations: 

  • Children – Identify and vaccinate children who are not up to date with their MMR vaccines. All children should receive two doses of MMR vaccine. A health care professional should administer the first dose to children at 12 to 15 months old and the second at 4 to 6 years old.
    • Children 6 to 11 months old who will be traveling internationally or domestically to a region with a known active measles outbreak should receive one dose of MMR vaccine, per the Maine CDC’s expanded recommendations for those traveling to a destination with a known outbreak. This dose is not considered part of the routine two-dose series starting at age 12 months.  
  • Adults – All adults should have proof of immunity to measles. Acceptable proof includes one of the following:
    • written documentation of vaccination
    • laboratory evidence of immunity
    • birth before 1957
    • or laboratory confirmation of disease
    • individuals who received a measles vaccine between 1963 to 1967 are encouraged to speak with their doctor to determine if additional vaccination is needed. Those known to have received an inactivated dose measles vaccine should receive a single dose of MMR. Five percent of people who received measles vaccine between 1963 and 1967 received an inactivated vaccine.

For adults with no evidence of immunity to measles, the U.S. CDC recommends one dose of MMR vaccine as soon as possible. Adults who are traveling domestically or internationally to a region known to have an active measles outbreak should receive two doses of the vaccine. Pregnant women should not receive any live virus vaccine during pregnancy, including MMR.

Vaccination Information:

  • Two doses of MMR vaccine are about 97% effective at preventing measles; one dose is about 93% effective.
  • The U.S. CDC considers people who received two doses of MMR vaccine as a child protected for life. 
  • Some people exposed to the virus may still get measles even if they got the MMR vaccine. In this case, they are more likely to have a milder illness and are also less likely to spread the disease to other people.

For More Information:

  • The Maine CDC’s measles webpage: http://www.maine.gov/dhhs/measles
  • The U.S. CDC’s measles webpage: http://www.cdc.gov/measles/index.html
  • The Maine Immunization Program webpage: https://www.maine.gov/dhhs/mecdc/infectious-disease/immunization/

items.content_text:
AUGUSTA, MAINE
– Absentee voting by mail will continue just as it has in prior elections, announced Secretary of State Shenna Bellows today.  The US Supreme Court rejected the US Postal Service and Trump Administration’s quest to change the rules for mailed ballots.  States including the State of Maine had filed a lawsuit to challenge the Trump Executive Order and US Postal Service rule that would have dramatically limited the ability of clerks to mail ballots to voters.  A lower court blocked the rule on constitutional grounds, and the US Supreme Court denied the Trump Administration’s attempt to overturn the lower court.
“This is good news for voters and for democracy.  Voters can rest assured that they have all of the same options for absentee voting including receiving and returning their ballot by mail that they have had in every other election,” said Secretary of State Shenna Bellows.  “We know that many Mainers – particularly seniors and people with disabilities – appreciate the convenience of voting from home, and we are thrilled that our joint legal efforts with states across the country to protect the right to vote by mail have succeeded.”
Voters can request absentee ballots utilizing the Secretary of State’s online
absentee ballot portal
, in writing, or by calling their
municipal clerk
directly. Absentee voting in Maine begins October 5, and voters should start receiving their ballots in the mail in the first week of October. Voters can track the status of their absentee ballot via Maine’s
online absentee ballot tracking portal
.

AUGUSTA, MAINE – Today, September 15, is National Voter Registration Day, a nonpartisan civic holiday dedicated to celebrating democracy and registering voters.

"Registering to vote is the first step for every citizen to participate in our democracy and have your voice heard," said Secretary of State Shenna Bellows. "We like to say that every day in Maine is voter registration day because in our state you can even register to vote on Election Day, but this holiday is an important reminder of the fundamental right to vote and have your voice heard."

Secretary Bellows will visit voter registration events around the state today to speak with Mainers about the importance of registering to vote. She is available to do in interviews upon request.

To register to vote in Maine, voters must be Maine residents, U.S. citizens, and at least 16 years old, though only Mainers who will be 18 years old on or before November 3, 2026 may vote in the General Election. When registering for the first time, voters must provide proof of residency and identity. Current or former incarceration status does not disqualify any Mainer from registering to vote or casting their ballot. Incarcerated persons at a correctional facility or county jail may register to vote in the Maine municipality where they established residency prior to incarceration.

Maine does not currently offer a voter registration lookup tool, but voters can contact their town or city clerk if they are unsure if they are already registered to vote, or if their information is up-to-date. Contact information for municipal clerks and registrars is available at https://www.maine.gov/sos/cec/elec/munic.html.

Maine has same day voter registration, meaning that Mainers may register to vote and cast their ballot on the same day, even Election Day. Online voter registration at maine.gov/vote is available through 5 pm on October 13 (21 days before Election Day). Registrations done by mail need to be received by the municipal clerk of the voter by that date as well. Automatic voter registration during Bureau of Motor Vehicle transactions is available through October 27 (7 days before Election Day). After those deadlines, registrations must be done in person at the voter’s municipality.

items.title: US Department of Labor investigation finds Chicago construction employer exposed workers to continued safety hazards, proposes $265K in penalties — U.S. Department of Labor — News Releases
items.content_text: CHICAGO – The U.S. Department of Labor has cited a Calumet City-based residential construction and carpentry employer after two separate investigations into its continued failure to provide fall protection for workers. The department’s Occupational Safety and Health Administration investigated two worksites operated by Martin Araujo – doing business as Araujo Construction Corp. – and found that carpenters and general construction laborers were installing roof rafters and roof sheeting without fall protection, exposing them to falls of up to 25 feet. OSHA cited Araujo Construction with two willful violations for not providing fall protection, while working from heights during residential construction at the two worksites. OSHA also cited the employer with nine repeat safety violations for failing to provide head and eye protection, lacking handrails on stairways, and failing to make sure ladders extended three feet above access areas. Additionally, OSHA issued a serious violation to Araujo Construction for not having safe access to a platform, and an other-than-serious violation for lacking training certifications. OSHA proposed $265,868 in combined penalties.Martin Araujo has 15 business days from receipt of its citations and penalties to comply, request an informal conference with OSHA’s area director, or contest the findings before the independent Occupational Safety and Health Review Commission. items.title: US Department of Labor debars Louisiana employer from H-2A visa program for federal violations — U.S. Department of Labor — News Releases
items.content_text: NEW ORLEANS – The U.S. Department of Labor debarred a Calcasieu Parish farmer from participating in the H-2A visa program for one year, after an investigation discovered multiple violations under the H-2A program.The department’s Wage and Hour Division determined that Jevon Natali, operating as Jevon Natali Farms near Lake Charles, violated H-2A program requirements when it misrepresented the actual terms and conditions of employment on its submitted job order. The H-2A visa program allows agricultural employers who anticipate a shortage of domestic workers to bring nonimmigrant foreign workers to the U.S. to perform agricultural labor of a temporary or seasonal nature. The one-year debarment prohibits the employer from hiring workers through the program during that period because of the seriousness of the violations.“Employers who abuse the H-2A program should expect to be held accountable for their actions,” said Wage and Hour Division District Director Troy Mouton in New Orleans. “Debarment sends a clear message that the Department of Labor will protect the integrity of this program and safeguard opportunities for American workers.”Division investigators also found Fair Labor Standards Act violations when Jevon Natali Farms failed to pay the required overtime premium of time-and-one-half employees’ regular rates of payfor non-agricultural work performed over 40 hours in a workweek. Jevon Natali Farms also failed to provide paystubs with the required information.Employees and employers can contact the Wage and Hour Division with questions and requests for compliance assistance at its toll-free helpline, 866-4US-WAGE (487-9243). Employers are encouraged to use the agency’s industry-specific compliance assistance toolkits to learn about their responsibilities under the laws enforced by the division.

Hello, this is Governor Janet Mills, and thank you for listening.

Robert and Jackie Norton's son was waiting for them in California 25 years ago. He was about to get married, but his parents, a retired couple from Lubec, never made it to the ceremony. Their plane, American Airlines Flight 11, hit the North Tower of the World Trade Center in a horrific act of terrorism on September 11, 2001.

Katie Ward, the sister of Stephen Ward, said her brother couldn't wait to take over the big city when he moved to New York. A native of Gorham, Maine, Stephen had big plans, and he encouraged everyone to go after what they wanted and live their best lives. Stephen was working on the 101st floor of the North Tower at the World Trade Center that fateful day.

Robert Jalbert was raised in Lewiston and lived in Swampscott, Massachusetts, when he boarded United Flight 175 for a business trip to California. People described him as an easygoing guy, a good friend, and a proud father who went to church every Sunday and served as a Eucharistic Minister. His flight struck the South Tower of the World Trade Center.

Attorney Jim Roux of Portland, someone who loved hiking Mount Washington. He was also on United Flight 175. Through this Saturday, September 12th, the summit of Mount Washington will be lit by two pillars of light that will be visible from 100 miles away to honor Jim Roux and the thousands of others whose lives were cut short that day.

Commander Robert Schlegel was a devoted husband, a decorated officer, and an avid ice hockey and football player. Originally from Gray, Maine, Commander Schlegel had been awarded the Purple Heart and other medals for his career-long service in the U.S. Navy. He had been promoted just a month before he boarded American Airlines Flight 77, which was then flown into the Pentagon, killing all on board.

25 years ago, Maine and the nation were forever changed by the September 11th terrorist attacks. On this solemn anniversary, I join the Maine people in pausing to remember the nearly 3,000 souls taken from us that day, including the six beloved people from Maine. And in saluting the courageous first responders who rushed towards danger, including those heroes still living with devastating health conditions caused by exposure to toxic flames and fumes.

One of those firefighters moved to Falmouth, Maine. Kevin Hogan wasn't working on September 11, but when the first plane struck the World Trade Center, he jumped into a pickup truck, heading to Ground Zero. Through a storm of ash, he and other firefighters searched for scraps of clothing and under rubble, praying to find and return loved ones to their families. So today, we recognize first responders like Kevin, and we also thank the many servicemembers who stepped up to keep our nation safe then and in the years since.

And we thank our friends in other countries who stood by us. On September 11, more than 250 flights were forced to divert to Canada, including 38 commercial flights that touched down in Gander, Newfoundland, when more than 7,000 passengers were stranded. A local TV station put out a call to "lend a hand, do what you can," and residents opened their homes to Americans in need. Now, more than ever before, we should remember that kindness of our neighbors to the North. 

Although more than a hundred million Americans are too young to remember that dark day, today, we take a moment to remember and to honor those who perished that day, as well as the first responders who ran towards danger and stayed through the devastating aftermath, and the men and women who stepped up and who continue to step up to keep us safe.

This is Governor Janet Mills, and on behalf of the 1.4 million people of the state of Maine, we honor those who perished, those who helped, those who stood by us, 25 years ago, September 11, 2001.

items.title: Maine Wasted Food Prevention Week - September 28 through October 4 — Governor of Maine — Official Documents (Executive Orders)
items.content_text:
WHEREAS
, food is one of Maine’s most valuable resources and is essential for the health and nutrition of all our 1.4 million residents; and
WHEREAS
, nearly 40 percent of food produced in Maine is never eaten – over 361,000 tons annually – primarily ending up in landfills where it produces dangerous methane gas which is 28 times more potent than carbon dioxide and a major contributor to climate change; and
WHEREAS
, Maine people can save money by preventing wasted food, with the average Maine family spending nearly $3,000 annually on food that is thrown away; and
WHEREAS
, over 80 percent of consumers misunderstand food date labels causing large amounts of perfectly good food to be thrown away in homes, businesses, and even food pantries; and
WHEREAS
, Maine communities can substantially reduce their waste disposal costs by preventing wasted food since food is the single largest municipal solid waste component; and
WHEREAS
, Maine K-12 schools have a special role in educating our next generation to reduce, recover, and recycle the estimated 7 million pounds of school food wasted annually; and
WHEREAS
, we can help our farmers, strengthen our local food systems, and conserve our natural resources – water, air, energy, and land – by valuing Maine food and composting food scraps instead of wasting it as trash;
NOW THEREFORE
, be it resolved that I, Janet T. Mills, Governor of the State of Maine, do hereby proclaim the week of September 28-October 4, 2026, as
Maine Wasted Food Prevention Week
and I encourage all Maine people to become aware of the wasted food in our homes, schools and all around us, and to commit to stop throwing food away.
In testimony whereof, I have caused
the Great Seal of the State to be
hereunto affixed GIVEN under my
hand at Augusta this second day
of September Two Thousand Twenty-Six

Registration is Open for the 2026 MaineCare Provider Conference

Sep 10, 2026

Join colleagues from across Maine for the inaugural 2026 MaineCare Provider Conference—a dynamic day of learning, collaboration, and connection. Centered on the theme "Stronger Together: Navigating Change Through Collaboration," this conference brings together providers from across the MaineCare community to share innovative practices, explore emerging challenges, and strengthen partnerships that improve care for the people we serve. 

This conference is made possible through support from Maine's Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP), a federal initiative that helps strengthen rural healthcare by improving access to care, supporting the healthcare workforce, modernizing healthcare systems, and advancing innovative models of care across the state. The conference reflects these goals by creating opportunities for providers to learn from one another, build stronger partnerships, and share strategies that improve care for MaineCare members. 

Designed for professionals across primary care, behavioral health, oral health, community support services, and other disciplines, the conference features interactive presentations, practical strategies, and real-world solutions that participants can immediately apply in their work. Whether you're looking to expand your knowledge, exchange ideas with peers, or build new connections across Maine's healthcare and social service systems, this conference offers valuable opportunities to learn from one another and shape the future of care. 

The conference welcomes participants in all roles with MaineCare provider organizations, including: 

  • Clinicians 
  • Administrators 
  • Care coordinators 
  • Program staff 
  • Quality improvement professionals 
  • Other team members who support MaineCare members 

Together, we'll explore approaches that strengthen the healthcare workforce, improve access to care, enhance member engagement, and support better health outcomes for MaineCare members across the state. 

Provider Conference Details 

Date: October 27, 2026 

Time: 9:00 AM – 3:00 PM (Registration, Poster Session, and Networking time begins at 8:00 AM) 

Place: Augusta Civic Center, Community Drive, Augusta, ME 

Cost: Free!  

Space is limited, so register now!  

Some Providers Are Required to Participate – See the Special Code 

If you are a Delivery System Reform Unit (DSRU) provider including: 

  • Behavioral Health Homes 
  • Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinics 
  • Community Care Teams 
  • MaineMOM 
  • Opioid Health Homes 
  • Primary Care Plus 

MaineCare policy requires at least one member of your care team to attend this department-sponsored learning activity.  

The registration code specifically designated for DSRU providers to help account for required participation is DSRUPROVIDER. Click the “reserve a spot” button on the registration page, and enter this code into the promo code box, to ensure you can access the reserved DSRU tickets. 

For questions about this conference, please contact MaineCare’s communication team.

items.title: Hazardous Materials: Notice of Administrative Determination of Preemption for Common Law Tort Claims Concerning the Transportation of Gasoline — Federal Register — Documents Matching 'Maine'
items.content_text: The Exxon Mobil Corporation (Exxon) seeks a determination that Federal law preempts State common law claims brought against it in New Jersey concerning the safe transportation of gasoline in commerce. PHMSA is issuing a final administrative determination concluding that the State common law tort claims presented by Exxon are preempted. Each of these duties, if imposed, would present an obstacle to compliance with the Federal regulatory framework essential for the safe transportation of gasoline. In addition, any claims about covered subjects, such as the marking, loading and unloading, and classification of gasoline that are not substantively the same as the applicable HMR provisions are preempted.
